implementation_notes: Boost.DLL wraps the platform linker (dlopen/LoadLibrary) in a RAII shared_library with reference counting, and import<T>()/import_alias<T>() resolve a symbol into a typed callable, so the configurator's link step becomes a constructor call and a typed import. The library keeps the loaded object alive while it is in scope or while the imported symbol is used, and unload callbacks can be registered to run teardown before the library leaves the address space; use import_class for C++ classes or import_alias to bind C++-mangled names when an extern "C" entry point is not available.
pitfalls: Unloading runs the library's termination routines: keep the shared_library (or its refcounted alias) alive for as long as any symbol obtained from it can be called, and never store only the imported function pointer.
Plain import() looks up C symbols; C++ components need an extern "C" factory entry point or Boost.DLL's mangled import/import_class, and compilers differ in mangling (MSVC vs Itanium).
On Linux, several components exporting the same symbol names shadow each other depending on load order and RTLD_GLOBAL/RTLD_LOCAL; give components unique prefixes or load them in separate namespaces.

variants.name: ACE Service Configurator framework (the POSA2 reference realization)
variants.implementation_notes: POSA2's reference implementation is the ACE Service Configurator framework: ACE_Service_Object is the Component with init/suspend/resume/fini lifecycle hooks, ACE_Service_Repository is the repository that tracks loaded services by name, and ACE_Service_Config parses the configuration file (dynamic/static directives, suspend, resume, remove) and drives the framework's Reactor and Service Repository. Choose it when ACE's other services (Reactor, Acceptor-Connector, logging) are already in the stack and a battle-tested, policy-rich configurator matters more than a small dependency footprint.
pitfalls: ACE brings its own reactor, service repository and configuration syntax; mixing it with a second configuration mechanism in the same process creates two sources of truth for which services are loaded.
ACE's 'remove' detaches a service from the repository but keeps the dynamically linked library mapped, so resource reclamation still depends on the platform linker's reference counting.

variants.name: hand-written wrapper facade over dlopen/dlsym
variants.implementation_notes: When no third-party dependency is acceptable, wrap the POSIX API in a small facade: an RAII handle type that dlopen()s with RTLD_NOW|RTLD_LOCAL, an extern "C" factory symbol resolved with dlsym(), and a std::unique_ptr<component> that owns the instance while a shared_ptr to the handle keeps the code mapped. The component contract is then a plain abstract class or a function table, and type safety is restored by hand - exactly the trade the C++ idioms make when a library like Boost.DLL or ACE is out of scope.
pitfalls: reinterpret_cast of a dlsym() result is only safe for a function pointer whose type you guarantee in the contract; keep the extern "C" signatures in a shared header used by both sides.
The shared_ptr-to-handle and the component instance must be released together: dropping the handle first unmaps the code that the instance's destructor is about to run.
